title: Queries, keys and values
summary: Each token gets three vectors from three learned matrices: a query (what it is looking for), a key (what it offers to be found by) and a value (what it passes along). Scores are query · key, softmax turns them into weights, and the output mixes the values. In matrix form: Q = X W_Q, K = X W_K, V = X W_V, out = softmax(Q Kᵀ) V.
llm_link: Every attention layer in a GPT is this computation, with W_Q, W_K and W_V learned during pretraining. Researchers who inspect trained models find heads with recognisable jobs, such as attending to the previous token, which emerge from training rather than being programmed.
key_ideas: Query: what this token is looking for. Key: what it advertises. Value: what it hands over if chosen.
Q = X W_Q, K = X W_K, V = X W_V: three ordinary learned weight matrices.
Scores Q Kᵀ have shape (T, T): rows are queries, columns are keys.
Separate queries and keys remove the automatic self-match; separate values let what gets a token found differ from what it contributes.
Only rule for shapes: queries and keys must share the width d_k.

quiz.q: X is (6, 16), W_Q and W_K are (16, 8) and W_V is (16, 10). Predict the shape of softmax(Q Kᵀ) V.
quiz.explain: Q Kᵀ is (6, 8) @ (8, 6) = (6, 6). Multiplying by V, which is (6, 10), gives (6, 10). The value width can differ from the query/key width.

quiz.q: Which pair must have the same width for attention to work?
quiz.explain: Each score is a dot product q · k, which needs vectors of equal length. Values are only mixed by the weights, so their width is free.

quiz.q: In the library analogy, what plays the role of the value?
options: The label on the book's spine
The content of the book you take home
The shelf the book sits on
quiz.explain: The query is your request, the key is the spine label you match against, and the value is what you actually take away once a book is chosen.

quiz.q: Why do separate W_Q and W_K matrices fix the "everyone looks at itself" problem of raw attention?
options: q_i · k_i is no longer a squared length, so a token is not automatically its own best match
They remove the diagonal of the score table
quiz.explain: With raw attention the diagonal score is x_i · x_i = |x_i|². With q_i = x_i W_Q and k_i = x_i W_K, the diagonal is just another learned score.

quiz.q: In a trained LLM, where do the query, key and value matrices of each attention layer come from?
options: They are written by hand by engineers
They are learned by gradient descent during pretraining, like every other weight
They are copied from the embedding table
quiz.explain: They start random and are adjusted, together with all other parameters, to make next-token prediction more accurate.

problems.title: Shape drill: Q, K, V and the scores
problems.prompt:
Predict every shape before printing. T = 5 tokens, d = 8, d_k = 4. The values here are all ones because only the shapes matter.

Rules: (a, b) @ (b, c) gives (a, c); .T swaps axes; softmax keeps the shape.
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    """Exponentiate, then divide by the total along one axis (you will write this yourself in 9.6)."""
    e = np.exp(x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

T, d, d_k = 5, 8, 4
X  = np.ones((T, d))
Wq = np.ones((d, d_k)); Wk = np.ones((d, d_k)); Wv = np.ones((d, d_k))
Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
A = softmax(Q @ K.T)

# Predict each shape as a tuple, e.g. (4, 3), BEFORE printing anything.
# Then check yourself with print(<expression>.shape).
answers = {
    "Wq": None,
    "Q": None,
    "K.T": None,
    "Q @ K.T": None,
    "Q[2] @ K.T": None,
    "V": None,
    "A @ V": None,
}

tests.name: shape of Wq
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['Wq']
real = np.shape(Wq)
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for Wq'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but Wq has shape {real}. A projection maps a d-wide embedding to a d_k-wide query, so it has d rows and d_k columns.'

tests.name: shape of Q
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['Q']
real = np.shape(Q)
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for Q'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but Q has shape {real}. (T, d) @ (d, d_k) gives (T, d_k): one query per token.'

tests.name: shape of K.T
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['K.T']
real = np.shape(K.T)
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for K.T'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but K.T has shape {real}. K is (T, d_k); the transpose swaps the axes.'

tests.name: shape of Q @ K.T
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['Q @ K.T']
real = np.shape(Q @ K.T)
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for Q @ K.T'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but Q @ K.T has shape {real}. (T, d_k) @ (d_k, T) gives (T, T): one score for every (query, key) pair.'

tests.name: shape of Q[2] @ K.T
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['Q[2] @ K.T']
real = np.shape(Q[2] @ K.T)
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for Q[2] @ K.T'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but Q[2] @ K.T has shape {real}. One query (d_k,) against all keys (d_k, T) gives T scores.'

tests.name: shape of V
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['V']
real = np.shape(V)
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for V'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but V has shape {real}. (T, d) @ (d, d_k) gives one value per token.'

tests.name: shape of A @ V
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['A @ V']
real = np.shape(A @ V)
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for A @ V'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but A @ V has shape {real}. (T, T) @ (T, d_k) gives (T, d_k): one mixed value per token.'

hints: Q, K and V all have one row per token and d_k columns.
Q[2] is a single query of length d_k.

problems.title: One attention head (GPT, step 3)
problems.prompt:
Upgrade last lesson's raw attention to a real attention head. The starter contains your GPT so far: the tokenizer, the embedding table, and three projection matrices (random here; a trained model learns them).

Write attention_head(X, Wq, Wk, Wv) returning (out, A) with Q = X @ Wq, K = X @ Wk, V = X @ Wv, A = softmax(Q @ K.T) (each row) and out = A @ V.
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    """Exponentiate, then divide by the total along one axis (you will write this yourself in 9.6)."""
    e = np.exp(x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

# ---- the character-level GPT so far (lessons 9.1, 9.2) ----
text = "hello world"
vocab = sorted(set(text))
stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(vocab)}
def encode(s):
    return [stoi[ch] for ch in s]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, d_k = 8, 4
E = rng.normal(size=(len(vocab), d))           # embedding table (V, d)
X = E[np.array(encode("hello"))]               # (T, d) = (5, 8)
Wq = rng.normal(size=(d, d_k))                 # learned in a real model; random here
Wk = rng.normal(size=(d, d_k))
Wv = rng.normal(size=(d, d_k))

# ---- step 3: one attention head with queries, keys and values (this lesson) ----
def attention_head(X, Wq, Wk, Wv):
    """Returns (out, A). No scaling and no mask yet: those come in lesson 9.6."""
    # TODO 1: Q, K, V = three projections of X                 -> each (T, d_k)
    # TODO 2: A = softmax of each row of the (T, T) score table Q Kᵀ
    # TODO 3: out = A @ V                                       -> (T, d_k)
    pass

tests.name: shapes
tests.code:
import numpy as np
r=attention_head(X,Wq,Wk,Wv)
assert r is not None, 'return (out, A)'
out,A=r
assert A.shape==(5,5), f'A should be (T, T) = (5, 5), got {A.shape}'
assert out.shape==(5,4), f'out should be (T, d_k) = (5, 4): one mixed value per token; got {out.shape}'

tests.name: rows of A sum to 1
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out,A=attention_head(X,Wq,Wk,Wv)
assert np.allclose(A.sum(axis=1),1), f'rows of A must sum to 1, got {A.sum(axis=1).round(3)}; softmax along the last axis'

tests.name: uses queries and keys, not raw X
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out,A=attention_head(X,Wq,Wk,Wv)
ref=softmax((X@Wq)@(X@Wk).T)
assert np.allclose(A,ref), 'A should be softmax(Q @ K.T) with Q = X @ Wq and K = X @ Wk'

tests.name: mixes the values
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out,A=attention_head(X,Wq,Wk,Wv)
assert np.allclose(out,A@(X@Wv)), 'out should be A @ V with V = X @ Wv (the values are mixed, not X itself)'

tests.name: raw attention is the special case W = I
tests.code:
import numpy as np
I=np.eye(8)
out,A=attention_head(X,I,I,I)
ref=softmax(X@X.T)
assert np.allclose(A,ref) and np.allclose(out,ref@X), 'with identity projections the head should reduce to last lesson\'s raw attention'

hints: Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
A = softmax(Q @ K.T, axis=-1); return A @ V, A
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    """Exponentiate, then divide by the total along one axis (you will write this yourself in 9.6)."""
    e = np.exp(x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

# ---- the character-level GPT so far (lessons 9.1, 9.2) ----
text = "hello world"
vocab = sorted(set(text))
stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(vocab)}
def encode(s):
    return [stoi[ch] for ch in s]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, d_k = 8, 4
E = rng.normal(size=(len(vocab), d))           # embedding table (V, d)
X = E[np.array(encode("hello"))]               # (T, d) = (5, 8)
Wq = rng.normal(size=(d, d_k))                 # learned in a real model; random here
Wk = rng.normal(size=(d, d_k))
Wv = rng.normal(size=(d, d_k))

# ---- step 3: one attention head with queries, keys and values (this lesson) ----
def attention_head(X, Wq, Wk, Wv):
    """Returns (out, A). No scaling and no mask yet: those come in lesson 9.6."""
    Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
    A = softmax(Q @ K.T, axis=-1)
    return A @ V, A

problems.title: Teach "it" to find "cat"
problems.prompt:
A trained model learns W_Q and W_K. Here you choose them by hand. Three tokens have 2-number embeddings; the first coordinate is a crude "noun-ness". With identity matrices (raw attention), it mostly attends to itself.

Change Wq and Wk (2 × 2 NumPy arrays) so that weights_for_it(Wq, Wk) puts more than half of the weight on cat. Think about what the keys should advertise and what the query of it should ask for.
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    """Exponentiate, then divide by the total along one axis (you will write this yourself in 9.6)."""
    e = np.exp(x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

# three tokens with 2-number embeddings
words = ["cat", "sat", "it"]
X = np.array([[1.0, 0.0],     # cat
              [0.0, 1.0],     # sat
              [0.6, 0.8]])    # it

def weights_for_it(Wq, Wk):
    Q, K = X @ Wq, X @ Wk
    return softmax(Q[2] @ K.T)          # how much "it" attends to cat, sat, it

# With identity matrices this is raw attention, and "it" mostly looks at itself:
#   print(weights_for_it(np.eye(2), np.eye(2)).round(2))
# TODO: choose 2x2 matrices so that "it" puts more than half its weight on "cat".
Wq = np.eye(2)
Wk = np.eye(2)

tests.name: it attends mostly to cat
tests.code:
import numpy as np
w=weights_for_it(np.asarray(Wq,float),np.asarray(Wk,float))
assert np.argmax(w)==0, f'the largest weight should be on cat (index 0); got weights {w.round(2)} for [cat, sat, it]'
assert w[0]>0.5, f'cat should get more than half the weight, got {w[0]:.2f}. Try making the keys exaggerate the noun coordinate.'

tests.name: matrices are 2 x 2
tests.code:
import numpy as np
assert np.shape(Wq)==(2,2) and np.shape(Wk)==(2,2), 'both projections map 2 numbers to 2 numbers, so they are 2 x 2'

hints: Scores are q_it · k_j. With Wq = I the query is just [0.6, 0.8]. Which keys would make cat's score large compared with it's own?
If the keys keep only the first coordinate and stretch it, cat's key becomes long while sat's vanishes.
Wk = np.array([[5.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]]) with Wq = np.eye(2) gives cat about 0.74.
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    """Exponentiate, then divide by the total along one axis (you will write this yourself in 9.6)."""
    e = np.exp(x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

# three tokens with 2-number embeddings
words = ["cat", "sat", "it"]
X = np.array([[1.0, 0.0],     # cat
              [0.0, 1.0],     # sat
              [0.6, 0.8]])    # it

def weights_for_it(Wq, Wk):
    Q, K = X @ Wq, X @ Wk
    return softmax(Q[2] @ K.T)          # how much "it" attends to cat, sat, it

# With identity matrices this is raw attention, and "it" mostly looks at itself:
#   print(weights_for_it(np.eye(2), np.eye(2)).round(2))
# TODO: choose 2x2 matrices so that "it" puts more than half its weight on "cat".
Wq = np.eye(2)
Wk = np.array([[5.0, 0.0],     # every key keeps 5x its first coordinate ("noun-ness")
               [0.0, 0.0]])    # and drops the second
